articles.content:
Her catchy videos have racked up billions of views, but Rachel Accurso’s statements on everything from Gaza to LGBTQ rights have caused a stir. She talks about screen time, song fatigue and speculation she might enter politics

T he YouTube star Ms Rachel, toddler whisperer extraordinaire, spots me before I clock her, and even from a distance and without her trademark pink T-shirt and denim dungarees, she is instantly recognisable by her wave, which is accompanied by an enthusiastic bounce. I half expect her to say, “Hi, friends”, as she does at the start of many of her videos. Instead she bounds over, wearing a classic off-duty mum uniform – Sesame Street sweatshirt, grey leggings, baseball cap that reads “Mama” – and removes her oversized sunglasses. She’s very sorry, she says, rubbing her eyes, that she is so tired – but her manner remains unfailingly, characteristically peppy.

It is only seven years since Rachel Accurso, who used to be a preschool music teacher, uploaded her first video to YouTube, a counting song for preschoolers called Bubble, Bubble Pop! . She and her husband, Aron Accurso, who worked as a music director on Broadway, made the video because their one-year-old son had a speech delay and there seemed to be a dearth of quality videos online that could help toddlers learn to speak.

Nowadays, the Ms Rachel YouTube channel has more than 21 million followers, and since she signed with Netflix in 2025, the series has been streamed more than 69m times, becoming the highest-ranked new kids’ TV show. You can buy Ms Rachel dolls, rattles, talking toy phones, books and pyjamas. The couple are releasing their first album this month.

Ms Rachel, who is 43 and has a 17-month-old daughter, Susannah, as well as her eight-year-old son, Thomas, has also amassed a huge following on Instagram (5.5 million) and TikTok (11 million), where the mums of her superfans congregate, and where she cuts a more controversial figure, having become a vocal opponent of the Israeli government over its war in Gaza, and a campaigner on other humanitarian issues, such as family immigration detention centres in the US and the war in Sudan. She champions LGBTQ rights, posts about the case for slavery reparations and free universal childcare, and is emerging as a hero of the American left. This month, when the rapper Macklemore pledged $1m to organisations supporting Palestine, Ms Rachel said she would match the donation and said every “wealthy white celebrity” should do the same. Earlier this year she was on the inauguration committee for Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s charismatic leftwing mayor. She has publicly endorsed other insurgent progressives, such as Abdul El-Sayed, who recently won the Democratic Senate primary in Michigan – making her a whole lot more political than any children’s presenter needs to be.

We are meeting in a park close to her in-laws’ home in Colorado, where she filmed during the pandemic, which is when Ms Rachel videos began taking off in a very big way. Her preschool fanbase are, of course, unaware of any of her politics, and they cannot get enough of her. Her videos use song and play to teach first words, early phonics and other essentials like potty training. One has been viewed over 2bn times, considerably more than the average Taylor Swift music video. Even the first clip she ever made has now been viewed 21m times. “That’s funny, because it’s not that good!” she jokes: she and Aron filmed it in their New York apartment with her phone balanced on a stack of books.

There’s often something mysterious about internet fame: in a crowded field of self-taught content creators, what distinguishes the star? Accurso sometimes cannot believe the twist her family’s life has taken. “If 10 years ago someone said, ‘You’re in Rolling Stone’, we’d be like, ‘For what?’ And if they said, ‘For The Wheels on the Bus and the Caterpillar song’, we’d be like, ‘What?! How did that happen?!’” she says.

But, though unpredictable, the couple’s success is hardly random. Accurso points out that they identified a niche, an untapped demand for educational content for toddlers, and that their videos were co-created with their early audience, who told them what they liked and what they wanted more of. “It almost feels like this live thing you’re creating with parents,” she says.

Then there’s the fact that if you set out to identify the perfect couple to make hit toddler TV, you would struggle to improve on Rachel and Aron Accurso. Consider their professional and academic backgrounds: she has two master’s degrees – in music education and early childhood education – and early learning professionals attest to the science behind her approach. In an era of screen-time shaming, the Accursos create shows that parents don’t feel guilty about letting their young kids watch.

And then there is Accurso’s personality, her wide-eyed warmth and wholesomeness. She seems to be the rare person who truly loves hanging out with kids – who is genuinely delighted to play not only with her own, or her friends’ children, but with any five-year-old.

She and her husband – who also just seems so freaking nice – have complementary personalities, she says. She’s always bursting with ideas; he knows how to winnow them down and organise a timeline. They call each other “instant oatmeal” and “slow-cook oatmeal” because, “I just want things fast and he takes his time,” she says. And this is “crazy”, she tells me, but once, long after they had established these nicknames, they were both making breakfast and she looked over and saw that he was stirring slow-cook porridge while she was making instant! They are ridiculously cute.

So why get involved in politics? Accurso says she was advised to keep quiet on political issues, and she fielded arguments that “didn’t feel right”, such as, “If you don’t say anything about anything controversial, you’ll help more kids, because more people will watch.” She has faced pushback from conservative parents over her support for LGBTQ rights, and for using they/them pronouns when introducing the musician Jules Hoffman, who is non-binary, but this has been eclipsed by the response to her criticism of the Israeli government.

Accurso says she witnessed footage from Gaza and spoke to families there, and cannot understand why anyone who has done the same would not feel moved to do all they can to stop the violence. “It’s good to criticise governments for violating children’s rights. It’s something that everyone should be doing. Because we’re the grownups of this world and we’re meant to keep children safe. And the fact that we are not is horrific,” she says.

From a pure business perspective, the advice about staying silent may have been right. When she began speaking out about the humanitarian toll on Gaza, the backlash, which included accusations of antisemitism, took her by surprise. “I was confused and devastated that people said because you care about children who are starving, and whose food is being blocked, you don’t care about these [Jewish] kids,” she says. “I was like, oh my gosh, I have a deep love for, a deep care for, all children.” She has posted messages of sympathy for Jewish victims, and has collaborated with groups such as Parents Circle, which works with Israeli and Palestinian families who have lost loved ones, and yet the public response to her work is as messy and heated as you’d expect: the pro-Israel group StopAntisemitism nominated her for antisemite of the year in 2025, although many other Jewish organisations have rallied in her defence. She says she has grown accustomed to the maelstrom. “I had this moment when I was praying to God, like how do I handle people hating me? And I feel like I got the message that our goal in life isn’t to be the most liked or the most loved,” she tells me. “It’s that you’re meant to help kids, and stand with kids, and speak the truth about things.”

Because of her outspokenness on Gaza, some Jewish parents have switched allegiance to Ms Sara, a kids’ YouTuber who even looks a lot like Ms Rachel – with the same long brunette hair and knotted headband – and who teaches Jewish culture and songs. “I think she’s wonderful!” Accurso says, when I mention her. “I’m never like, ‘Don’t watch this person – watch me’, at all.”

One of her more hardline public stances is her refusal to work with people who have not publicly spoken out in defence of civilians in Gaza. “I’m going to work with people who aren’t in a privileged position, because that’s not fair to them if they could lose the ability to put food on the table. But people who are privileged who don’t say anything? Yeah, I’m not interested in working with them. Because I feel like maybe if we all said something, the genocide would stop,” she explains.

Not everyone will agree with this analysis; where some hear compassion, others will diagnose political naivety. “Why are we starving kids when there’s enough food in the world? Why are kids in Sudan starving? Why are kids in the Congo facing sexual violence? They’re kids. I don’t understand. And why do we dehumanise other people when I just feel like every person is different in beautiful ways but also so similar? How could we not want to help everyone?” she asks at one point. Sometimes she says she feels as if she’s living in a “fake, surreal world” because she does not understand how we can tolerate so much unfairness and unchecked suffering. She thinks all elected politicians should be forced to meet children like Rahaf, a three-year-old Gazan amputee she invited on the Ms Rachel show, so they understand the stakes. So is she naive, or is politics too unfeeling?

“I just have a really good moral compass,” she tells me at one point. Which may be why, for all the controversy, she says she is often approached and thanked by strangers on the street, and she enjoys a lot of breathless, all-caps online support. “Ms Rachel for president,” her supporters sometimes write underneath her posts. When the Democratic candidate Graham Platner dropped out of the Maine Senate race after being accused of sexual assault, Accurso – who is from Maine – was spoken of as the dream candidate for Democrats there. “That’s hilarious,” she says. She has no interest in entering politics. But, she adds, sounding unusually tentative because “maybe everyone will be upset”, she hopes to one day become a Christian minister. One thing you need to know about Ms Rachel is that she’s the kind of person who prays every day for the people who hate her.

A ccurso says she was “born spiritual”. She was raised in small-town Maine by a single mum, who dropped out of university when Accurso’s elder sister was born, but later retrained as a social worker and was often juggling multiple jobs. Her mother remains her lodestar, and she named her daughter – born via surrogate in 2025 – after her. It was “rough at times”, growing up with little money, and Accurso felt rejected by her father and used to wonder why he didn’t seem to want her. That said, her mother surrounded her with “so much unconditional love”. She watched her mum shovel snow and build a treehouse and fix the plumbing by herself, and it expanded her own ambitions. It also shaped her politics. “All my experiences have led me to knowing we should take care of each other,” she says.

Accurso was an anxious child, who by seven or eight was showing signs of OCD, flicking her light switch on and off to ward off trouble. She felt things deeply. Her mother has kept a note of how, at three, when she heard her neighbour was killing ants she exclaimed, “Don’t kill ants! Let them be free and feel the world!” When her mother could not take her to church because she had a new weekend job at Pizza Hut, Accurso, though only nine, went by herself. She didn’t join the children’s Sunday school but sat through the sermon for adults, praying and trying to “figure things out”.

As a young adult she considered joining the seminary, but while working at a school for children with disabilities she felt “led” in a new direction. She formed a close bond with a child with cerebral palsy who was nonverbal, and her supervisor told her she had a “rare talent” for connecting with kids. Galvanised, she went into teaching, and later enrolled for a master’s at New York University, where she wrote a thesis on how to use songwriting to empower children going through hardship. She joined the Unitarian church when she moved to the city – it had a preschool attached and she figured she might get work there. The first time she went, someone offered to introduce her to “the best musician in the world”, and Aron Accurso ambled over.

Aron, who loved her smile, offered to walk her out, asked for her number, and made her wait a torturous three days before inviting her on a date, where she ate shrimp for the first time and thought, as they talked about music, that he might be her future husband. On their third date, she asked him if he liked Mr Rogers, the gentle, cardigan-wearing children’s TV presenter, and – what do you know? – he loves him, too. The couple married in 2016. “I feel like our souls are totally meant to be together,” she says.

Rachel and Aron had always enjoyed being “silly” together, and at first their Ms Rachel videos felt like “play”, but during the pandemic, when Accurso was teaching on Zoom, and Aron was stuck at home because theatres were closed, and parents were wondering how on earth to entertain their children through long lockdown days, things started taking off. Accurso soon received offers from executives hoping to buy the company. She would sit through meetings hosted by a “bunch of men” with ideas for how to commercialise the project and, although she was suspicious of their lack of interest in the educational side of her work, it was Aron who kept reminding her that she didn’t need their expertise. “Forever, I thought I was going to be replaced as the host,” she says. “Once we had millions and millions of views I thought, oh, maybe a real TV place will get a real actor and see that this was a good concept.” For years she felt as if she was just some “35-year-old mom”, a stand-in for the real, professional Ms Rachel. “We didn’t know that toddler TV could be big business,” she says.

The Accursos say their wealth is nowhere near the figures circulating online – I saw $50m – and most of their profits are put back into the company. Still, the couple must have more money than they ever imagined – enough that, on top of their recent $1m donation to Palestinian charities, the Accursos donated $1m to the World Food Programme in 2025. “My spirit doesn’t want to ever …” she says, struggling to express herself. “Well, I don’t have any fancy things, I could say that.” Oh, come off it, I say, but a bit more politely: what’s the fanciest thing you’ve bought yourself? “I like to buy toys … I think toys are fun, little fidget toys and stuff,” she replies. She has a cupboard filled with gifts in her house, so that any child who visits can pick out something for themself. That doesn’t count, I say. Have you ever bought yourself an expensive handbag? She only has one handbag, she says, because she has ADHD and has learned that if she has more than one, she loses important stuff. What about a fancy car? Nope. House? “I think space in New York is hard to come by and space is nice, but I don’t want a fancy house.”

“O h no!” Accurso suddenly exclaims, when we have been speaking for almost 90 minutes, and Aron is due to join us in the park. She is supposed to be talking about her album and she has been going off on all these tangents! Aron arrives a few minutes later, blond and very blue-eyed in a blue button-down shirt and smart linen trousers – they have taken a very different approach to dressing for this interview, she jokes with him as he approaches.

The forthcoming album, I’m So Happy, is Aron’s passion project. The couple had received business advice that they should scrape their most popular songs from YouTube and get the thing out as soon as possible – but Aron wanted to devote “extra care” to the album. He ended up collaborating with 19 singers and 42 instrumentalists, and worked with Michael Starobin, who has orchestrated several Disney films. “I really believe that kids respond to it, and kids deserve that kind of rich, beautiful music,” Aron says. Among the 23 tracks are classic nursery rhymes, like The Wheels on the Bus, and songs written by the Accursos themselves, including Caterpillar, a surprisingly affecting tune Aron wrote while trying to get their son to sleep. Whenever they play the song for their children, everyone starts weeping, and I must confess that when I listened ahead of the interview I grew teary, too. “Every day you’re growing bigger, you once were a little guy, but caterpillar, caterpillar, soon you’re going to fly,” it goes. (OK, I know. But, trust me, try listening to it.)

The musical flourishes are a boon for parents, who will inevitably hear these songs on infinite loop – more than any human should ever have to listen to anything, I say, experiencing a sudden intrusive memory of My First Album by Peppa Pig. “When your child is having fun, you’re having fun,” Accurso replies, because that is the kind of pure-hearted person she is. But then she does mention this one annoying song that Thomas really latched on to when he was two … before requesting this detail be removed from public record because she doesn’t want to be mean.

An album also has the advantage of allowing children to enjoy Ms Rachel without looking at a screen, I suggest. That’s true, Accurso says, but she does think we’re too hard on parents (and on ourselves) about screen time. “There’s a lot of judgment and shaming of parents, and I think if you understood what most parents are going through, that wouldn’t be there,” she says. She is not exactly a neutral party to the screen-time debate – toddler screen time is how she pays the bills – but she points out, quite fairly, that sometimes we all need our kids to veg out in front of the TV so that we can get stuff done. It can also be a useful tool for children with additional needs. It was a “gamechanger” for her son, who was too busy charging around to listen to Accurso as she followed after him, instructing him to “say Mama”; but when she was on a screen teaching him how to articulate his first words, he focused.

So, what are her screen-time rules, I ask. “Rules?!” she exclaims, sounding confused. “Just kidding!” Although her daughter loves singing with them both, sometimes the only thing that will calm her down on planes is watching Ms Rachel on TV. That morning, Accurso let her watch Daniel Tiger’s Neighbourhood, a cartoon inspired by Mr Rogers, so that Susie would stop trying to do dangerous stuff while Accurso was getting Thomas ready for summer camp. Susie is “such a sweet baby, but she has a hitting problem”, Accurso says, and this morning’s episode was about feeling mad. Susie has made progress, of sorts. Now, after she has hit someone, she says, “I’m mad.”

Accurso seems more relaxed – and goofier – with Aron present. At one point she slumps over the table, and he asks if she’s OK. “Just looking at a spider! Keep going!” she says. “You focus, and I’ll be the ADHD person.” Ms Rachel’s political profile must have taken a toll on the whole family. They have had security problems that they don’t want to go into. “We’re learning how to deal with that,” is all Aron says. When I ask if he ever wished for Accurso to stop talking about controversial issues, he replies that her compassion and empathy are “genuine” and are “something I fell in love with and admire about Rachel”. There was no question of stopping her, because if she didn’t stand up for her values, she wouldn’t be Rachel, he adds. “Aww, thank you, Aron,” she coos, reaching for his hand, “that is so sweet.”

Accurso still suffers from anxiety and OCD, struggling with intrusive thoughts, but her health is well managed with medication and therapy. It helps that she is learning that the internet is “not real life”, and that she doesn’t need to listen to the online vitriol. This morning, she received an email warning her of some new online nastiness about her, and she decided to simply not look.

I noticed when I scrolled through her Instagram and trawled through the comments that I started to feel anxious myself, imagining the extraordinary pressure she is under. The pressure comes not only from the hatred but from the adulation, the weight of expectations, the requests for help. I read a message from someone who said they had designed a headstone in her likeness for their one-year-old who had died unexpectedly, and could they show her a picture?

Then there is the immense responsibility that comes from having such a large platform. In January 2026, screenshots circulated showing that she had liked the comment “Free America from the Jews”, under a post she had shared that read “Free Palestine, Free Sudan, Free Congo, Free Iran”. Rachel issued a tearful apology, explaining that she had clicked “like” accidentally when she was trying to delete the remark. She shared a screenshot of the private conversation she had with a follower who drew attention to her like, which supported her version of events: “Ya I believe I deleted that earlier right when I saw it! I hate antisemitism,” she wrote.

“After that I got a turtle puppet,” she says, momentarily confusing me – does she mean some kind of automatic moderation software? Before I can ask an embarrassingly stupid question, she clarifies that she literally means a turtle toy. She and Susie were playing with it, “and I was like, I need to slow down like this turtle because I can’t afford to make a mistake like that again”.

She tries, as much as any supercelebrity can, to keep her focus on her family. She and Aron had always assumed they would have kids right away, but they struggled with fertility for years. Thomas, Ms Rachel’s first muse, has overcome his early speech struggles. He likes to deliver lectures to his parents that he closes with a professional, “Any questions?” Susie is currently Christmas-obsessed – Accurso recently found herself Googling short-sleeved Santa costumes, until it struck her that that isn’t a thing – and is “so cute and aggressive”. Having a toddler in the house again is, of course, providing inspiration for the show. They need to do something new about boo-boos, Accurso says, and another bathtime song and, yes, definitely, something about how it’s not OK to hit.

One of her more hardline public stances is her refusal to work with people who have not publicly spoken out in defence of civilians in Gaza. “I’m going to work with people who aren’t in a privileged position, because that’s not fair to them if they could lose the ability to put food on the table. But people who are privileged who don’t say anything? Yeah, I’m not interested in working with them. Because I feel like maybe if we all said something, the genocide would stop,” she explains.

Not everyone will agree with this analysis; where some hear compassion, others will diagnose political naivety. “Why are we starving kids when there’s enough food in the world? Why are kids in Sudan starving? Why are kids in the Congo facing sexual violence? They’re kids. I don’t understand. And why do we dehumanise other people when I just feel like every person is different in beautiful ways but also so similar? How could we not want to help everyone?” she asks at one point. Sometimes she says she feels as if she’s living in a “fake, surreal world” because she does not understand how we can tolerate so much unfairness and unchecked suffering. She thinks all elected politicians should be forced to meet children like Rahaf, a three-year-old Gazan amputee she invited on the Ms Rachel show, so they understand the stakes. So is she naive, or is politics too unfeeling?

“I just have a really good moral compass,” she tells me at one point. Which may be why, for all the controversy, she says she is often approached and thanked by strangers on the street, and she enjoys a lot of breathless, all-caps online support. “Ms Rachel for president,” her supporters sometimes write underneath her posts. When the Democratic candidate Graham Platner dropped out of the Maine Senate race after being accused of sexual assault, Accurso – who is from Maine – was spoken of as the dream candidate for Democrats there. “That’s hilarious,” she says. She has no interest in entering politics. But, she adds, sounding unusually tentative because “maybe everyone will be upset”, she hopes to one day become a Christian minister. One thing you need to know about Ms Rachel is that she’s the kind of person who prays every day for the people who hate her.

A ccurso says she was “born spiritual”. She was raised in small-town Maine by a single mum, who dropped out of university when Accurso’s elder sister was born, but later retrained as a social worker and was often juggling multiple jobs. Her mother remains her lodestar, and she named her daughter – born via surrogate in 2025 – after her. It was “rough at times”, growing up with little money, and Accurso felt rejected by her father and used to wonder why he didn’t seem to want her. That said, her mother surrounded her with “so much unconditional love”. She watched her mum shovel snow and build a treehouse and fix the plumbing by herself, and it expanded her own ambitions. It also shaped her politics. “All my experiences have led me to knowing we should take care of each other,” she says.

Accurso was an anxious child, who by seven or eight was showing signs of OCD, flicking her light switch on and off to ward off trouble. She felt things deeply. Her mother has kept a note of how, at three, when she heard her neighbour was killing ants she exclaimed, “Don’t kill ants! Let them be free and feel the world!” When her mother could not take her to church because she had a new weekend job at Pizza Hut, Accurso, though only nine, went by herself. She didn’t join the children’s Sunday school but sat through the sermon for adults, praying and trying to “figure things out”.

As a young adult she considered joining the seminary, but while working at a school for children with disabilities she felt “led” in a new direction. She formed a close bond with a child with cerebral palsy who was nonverbal, and her supervisor told her she had a “rare talent” for connecting with kids. Galvanised, she went into teaching, and later enrolled for a master’s at New York University, where she wrote a thesis on how to use songwriting to empower children going through hardship. She joined the Unitarian church when she moved to the city – it had a preschool attached and she figured she might get work there. The first time she went, someone offered to introduce her to “the best musician in the world”, and Aron Accurso ambled over.

Aron, who loved her smile, offered to walk her out, asked for her number, and made her wait a torturous three days before inviting her on a date, where she ate shrimp for the first time and thought, as they talked about music, that he might be her future husband. On their third date, she asked him if he liked Mr Rogers, the gentle, cardigan-wearing children’s TV presenter, and – what do you know? – he loves him, too. The couple married in 2016. “I feel like our souls are totally meant to be together,” she says.

Rachel and Aron had always enjoyed being “silly” together, and at first their Ms Rachel videos felt like “play”, but during the pandemic, when Accurso was teaching on Zoom, and Aron was stuck at home because theatres were closed, and parents were wondering how on earth to entertain their children through long lockdown days, things started taking off. Accurso soon received offers from executives hoping to buy the company. She would sit through meetings hosted by a “bunch of men” with ideas for how to commercialise the project and, although she was suspicious of their lack of interest in the educational side of her work, it was Aron who kept reminding her that she didn’t need their expertise. “Forever, I thought I was going to be replaced as the host,” she says. “Once we had millions and millions of views I thought, oh, maybe a real TV place will get a real actor and see that this was a good concept.” For years she felt as if she was just some “35-year-old mom”, a stand-in for the real, professional Ms Rachel. “We didn’t know that toddler TV could be big business,” she says.

The Accursos say their wealth is nowhere near the figures circulating online – I saw $50m – and most of their profits are put back into the company. Still, the couple must have more money than they ever imagined – enough that, on top of their recent $1m donation to Palestinian charities, the Accursos donated $1m to the World Food Programme in 2025. “My spirit doesn’t want to ever …” she says, struggling to express herself. “Well, I don’t have any fancy things, I could say that.” Oh, come off it, I say, but a bit more politely: what’s the fanciest thing you’ve bought yourself? “I like to buy toys … I think toys are fun, little fidget toys and stuff,” she replies. She has a cupboard filled with gifts in her house, so that any child who visits can pick out something for themself. That doesn’t count, I say. Have you ever bought yourself an expensive handbag? She only has one handbag, she says, because she has ADHD and has learned that if she has more than one, she loses important stuff. What about a fancy car? Nope. House? “I think space in New York is hard to come by and space is nice, but I don’t want a fancy house.”

“O h no!” Accurso suddenly exclaims, when we have been speaking for almost 90 minutes, and Aron is due to join us in the park. She is supposed to be talking about her album and she has been going off on all these tangents! Aron arrives a few minutes later, blond and very blue-eyed in a blue button-down shirt and smart linen trousers – they have taken a very different approach to dressing for this interview, she jokes with him as he approaches.

The forthcoming album, I’m So Happy, is Aron’s passion project. The couple had received business advice that they should scrape their most popular songs from YouTube and get the thing out as soon as possible – but Aron wanted to devote “extra care” to the album. He ended up collaborating with 19 singers and 42 instrumentalists, and worked with Michael Starobin, who has orchestrated several Disney films. “I really believe that kids respond to it, and kids deserve that kind of rich, beautiful music,” Aron says. Among the 23 tracks are classic nursery rhymes, like The Wheels on the Bus, and songs written by the Accursos themselves, including Caterpillar, a surprisingly affecting tune Aron wrote while trying to get their son to sleep. Whenever they play the song for their children, everyone starts weeping, and I must confess that when I listened ahead of the interview I grew teary, too. “Every day you’re growing bigger, you once were a little guy, but caterpillar, caterpillar, soon you’re going to fly,” it goes. (OK, I know. But, trust me, try listening to it.)

The musical flourishes are a boon for parents, who will inevitably hear these songs on infinite loop – more than any human should ever have to listen to anything, I say, experiencing a sudden intrusive memory of My First Album by Peppa Pig. “When your child is having fun, you’re having fun,” Accurso replies, because that is the kind of pure-hearted person she is. But then she does mention this one annoying song that Thomas really latched on to when he was two … before requesting this detail be removed from public record because she doesn’t want to be mean.

An album also has the advantage of allowing children to enjoy Ms Rachel without looking at a screen, I suggest. That’s true, Accurso says, but she does think we’re too hard on parents (and on ourselves) about screen time. “There’s a lot of judgment and shaming of parents, and I think if you understood what most parents are going through, that wouldn’t be there,” she says. She is not exactly a neutral party to the screen-time debate – toddler screen time is how she pays the bills – but she points out, quite fairly, that sometimes we all need our kids to veg out in front of the TV so that we can get stuff done. It can also be a useful tool for children with additional needs. It was a “gamechanger” for her son, who was too busy charging around to listen to Accurso as she followed after him, instructing him to “say Mama”; but when she was on a screen teaching him how to articulate his first words, he focused.

So, what are her screen-time rules, I ask. “Rules?!” she exclaims, sounding confused. “Just kidding!” Although her daughter loves singing with them both, sometimes the only thing that will calm her down on planes is watching Ms Rachel on TV. That morning, Accurso let her watch Daniel Tiger’s Neighbourhood, a cartoon inspired by Mr Rogers, so that Susie would stop trying to do dangerous stuff while Accurso was getting Thomas ready for summer camp. Susie is “such a sweet baby, but she has a hitting problem”, Accurso says, and this morning’s episode was about feeling mad. Susie has made progress, of sorts. Now, after she has hit someone, she says, “I’m mad.”

Accurso seems more relaxed – and goofier – with Aron present. At one point she slumps over the table, and he asks if she’s OK. “Just looking at a spider! Keep going!” she says. “You focus, and I’ll be the ADHD person.” Ms Rachel’s political profile must have taken a toll on the whole family. They have had security problems that they don’t want to go into. “We’re learning how to deal with that,” is all Aron says. When I ask if he ever wished for Accurso to stop talking about controversial issues, he replies that her compassion and empathy are “genuine” and are “something I fell in love with and admire about Rachel”. There was no question of stopping her, because if she didn’t stand up for her values, she wouldn’t be Rachel, he adds. “Aww, thank you, Aron,” she coos, reaching for his hand, “that is so sweet.”

Accurso still suffers from anxiety and OCD, struggling with intrusive thoughts, but her health is well managed with medication and therapy. It helps that she is learning that the internet is “not real life”, and that she doesn’t need to listen to the online vitriol. This morning, she received an email warning her of some new online nastiness about her, and she decided to simply not look.

I noticed when I scrolled through her Instagram and trawled through the comments that I started to feel anxious myself, imagining the extraordinary pressure she is under. The pressure comes not only from the hatred but from the adulation, the weight of expectations, the requests for help. I read a message from someone who said they had designed a headstone in her likeness for their one-year-old who had died unexpectedly, and could they show her a picture?

Then there is the immense responsibility that comes from having such a large platform. In January 2026, screenshots circulated showing that she had liked the comment “Free America from the Jews”, under a post she had shared that read “Free Palestine, Free Sudan, Free Congo, Free Iran”. Rachel issued a tearful apology, explaining that she had clicked “like” accidentally when she was trying to delete the remark. She shared a screenshot of the private conversation she had with a follower who drew attention to her like, which supported her version of events: “Ya I believe I deleted that earlier right when I saw it! I hate antisemitism,” she wrote.

“After that I got a turtle puppet,” she says, momentarily confusing me – does she mean some kind of automatic moderation software? Before I can ask an embarrassingly stupid question, she clarifies that she literally means a turtle toy. She and Susie were playing with it, “and I was like, I need to slow down like this turtle because I can’t afford to make a mistake like that again”.

She tries, as much as any supercelebrity can, to keep her focus on her family. She and Aron had always assumed they would have kids right away, but they struggled with fertility for years. Thomas, Ms Rachel’s first muse, has overcome his early speech struggles. He likes to deliver lectures to his parents that he closes with a professional, “Any questions?” Susie is currently Christmas-obsessed – Accurso recently found herself Googling short-sleeved Santa costumes, until it struck her that that isn’t a thing – and is “so cute and aggressive”. Having a toddler in the house again is, of course, providing inspiration for the show. They need to do something new about boo-boos, Accurso says, and another bathtime song and, yes, definitely, something about how it’s not OK to hit.

articles.title: Our children may be surprised by what’s in our will – should we tell them now? | Ask Annalisa Barbieri
articles.summary: You don’t have to reveal the contents, but I’ve seen families torn apart by unexpected inheritance plans My wife and I have three children and seve ral grandchildren. Our will may contain some surprises for them. Is it better to reveal its contents while we are still alive, or let our beneficiaries discover them when we die? We gave our children considerable financial help , enabling them to buy their first homes. We have also made sizeable contributions to our grandchildren’s education funds. Continue reading...
articles.content:
You don’t have to reveal the contents, but I’ve seen families torn apart by unexpected inheritance plans

My wife and I have three children and seve ral grandchildren. Our will may contain some surprises for them. Is it better to reveal its contents while we are still alive, or let our beneficiaries discover them when we die?

We gave our children considerable financial help , enabling them to buy their first homes. We have also made sizeable contributions to our grandchildren’s education funds.

Our thinking is that our descendants will need more assistance when they are young : for their education, setting up home, starting a family. And we want to give them the gift of knowing that my wife and I loved them enough to help with these challenges , and that the bequests came from us, not through the generosity of their parents.

My wife’s jewellery goes only to our granddaughters, and the mothers of our grandsons could feel aggrieved that their sons have been passed over. However, we don’t consider the jewellery to have any financial value, as it should never be exchanged for cash.

The financial value of our estate is to be divided one-third to each of the next three generations, with each third divided equally between the members of that generation. We have also stipulated that no generation’s members will receive more than their parent.

If we tell our children the contents of the will now, they may think we are asking for their opinions, which we emphatically are not. Making this clear may result in ill feeling. On the other hand, if they discover the will’s provisions only when we die, there may be room for misunderstanding, again resulting in ill feeling. We have explained our thinking in a document that accompanies the will. I wonder if others have wrestled with these questions and arrived at satisfactory conclusions?

I am assuming you live in England and Wales, where you can leave your estate to whomever you want.

I went to lawyer and wills specialist Gary Rycroft, who advised that “there is no legal requirement to tell anyone, including your children, what’s in your will. It is your money, your property and, ultimately, your decision. A will is not decided by a family committee.”

That said, Rycroft and I both advocate discussing things ahead of time. “I’m a fan of transparency,” said Rycroft. “No one likes surprises in wills, especially if the surprise is getting less than expected. And while the will is clear about who gets what, families can be left very unclear about why.”

So, yes, we think you should explain ahead of time. I have seen families torn asunder by unexpected wills. Also, who knows what might happen between now and when the will becomes active. What if you have an argument with a family member and they think the will is retribution (even if it was clearly dated before the row)? Also, remember that it is likely that either you or your wife will die first, so if you decide to talk about it beforehand, it’s best done together.

Rycroft said to make sure the extra document you mention is a “more formal ‘memorandum of wishes’. The will is still the legally operative document and the memorandum does not rewrite or trump it. Its value is in explaining the decisions.” This stands even if you have a meeting to explain, as people tend to forget what was said or recall only what they want to.

“Remember,” counselled Rycroft, “an inheritance is not just about what you leave behind. It’s also about how a person will be remembered.”

And don’t forget that anyone you leave things to who is over 18 can vary their inheritance, within a time limit, with a deed of variation and change who gets their share. A reminder that, after death, we cannot control those we leave behind.

articles.content:
If you’re a fresher, this may be the first time you’ve ever lived away from home. So how should you socialise, feed yourself and look after your health?

Y ou don’t realise until you leave home just how idiosyncratic every family is, and how many of its customs are tacit, invisible, or maintained by someone else. Now you’re among people who emphatically aren’t related to you. How would you have any idea which of your practices were universal, and which common courtesies your upbringing had totally skipped? How do you even know how to keep your own body and soul together without the behind-the-scenes input of parents, who also have peculiarities of their own? Here’s a starter pack on how to function.

Anything with blood goes at the bottom of the fridge (although fridge-sharing between vegetarians and meat-eaters should be negotiated first thing).

Refrigeration is a game-changing technology but it doesn’t work if you just leave food near the fridge, even for a couple of hours. Likewise, nothing that’s been defrosted should be frozen again.

Don’t put a cooked chicken on a board that hasn’t been washed since it had a raw chicken on it. Likewise, without getting overanxious about it, exercise caution around all raw meat. Don’t cross-contaminate utensils (that is, use the same knife on raw chicken and then salad, without washing it).

Hopefully, you won’t have a dishwasher, as washing-up is a life skill. But if you do, don’t put anything with an electrical plug in it.

Don’t use a wet cloth to protect your hands when you take things out of the oven. Use an oven glove.

Something quick that has protein in it and is not toast. Suggestion: an omelette.

Something that is a full meal, covers protein and vegetables, and can be eaten over several days. Suggestion: bolognese or vegetarian chilli .

Something that you can scale up to feed two or four without bankrupting yourself or showing off. Suggestion: pesto pasta, but please always add broccoli right at the end – such a small price to pay to not get scurvy.

Something that you can make for others that is comforting and nobody can take against or be allergic to. Suggestion: risotto .

Something that you can just pour boiling water over, like a cup of tea, only it’s food. Suggestion: miso soup or soba noodles.

It is actually quite hard to integrate fruit and vegetables into your diet if you’re cooking for yourself but don’t want to spend a lot of time on it. They don’t just magic themselves into food. You should keep a stock of things you can mainline raw while you’re doing something else – carrots, apples, tomatoes, cucumbers.

Everything is edible with the right chilli sauce: harissa, Tabasco, piripiri, sriracha, or for special occasions Hungarian pista or crispy prawn chilli oil. Likewise, pickles: lime pickle, gherkins, jalapeños.

You will probably be about 40 before you can be trusted to spontaneously grate ginger. Pastes in jars or tubes are a cheap alternative: arrive with one garlic and one ginger.

Dr Imogen Bloor, who recently retired as a full-time GP and clinical lead in London, is the source of this expertise.

Before you leave : make sure all your jabs are up to date, principally the new meningitis B vaccine and the five tetanus jabs you should have had during childhood. “Tetanus is incredibly rare, but if you get a wound, you’ll be much less anxious about it,” Bloor says.

“In the olden days, everyone had a Reader’s Digest Family Health Guide, and the internet has replaced that,” Bloor says. But the internet isn’t as easy to interpret. “You’re not born with the ability to separate the wheat from the chaff.” The NHS symptom checker and patient.info are the wheat. “Common things occur commonly – people latch on to likely cause #63. An 18-year-old with a hoarse voice almost certainly hasn’t got laryngeal cancer.”

If you were at home and something happened, you would ask a parent. So call a parent.

Pharmacists can see and treat a whole range of conditions, from hay fever to urinary tract infections. Calling 111 can be helpful, as they can provide advice and signpost you to appropriate services.

Is it freshers’ flu? “As a general principle, if you’ve got mild symptoms and you take paracetamol and fluids and you rest and things seem to improve, that’s a good sign.”

Or isn’t it freshers’ flu? “If you have a severe headache which isn’t relieved by simple pain relief, or if you’ve got associated symptoms, like loss of balance or confusion or altered consciousness, or you’re vomiting or you feel too unwell to get out of bed, then it is important to seek medical advice.”

Other red flags include: rapid onset, so if you feel a lot worse in a short time; a purpuric rash (one that doesn’t fade when you press on it – the classic meningitis symptom). Bloor remembers vividly from her sepsis awareness training “a number of patients who say, ‘I feel like I’m going to die.’ If you feel that ill, it’s more likely that you are really ill.”

If you get infected hair follicles or a boil on your butt (perianal abscess), don’t be too embarrassed to go to the doctor; it won’t get better on its own. Bloor has seen a lot of young people who depilate their pubes, and boys their chests, and it’s really easy to get an infection there if you don’t clean and exfoliate properly.

You don’t need a GP referral to use a sexual health or family planning clinic – just look up where it is. When you get there, be frank. “You can’t shock a doctor; most doctors have seen most things. It’s human and natural to feel shy or embarrassed but you’ve got to try not to worry about that.”

If you think you might be so drunk you have to go to A&E, you’re probably lucid enough that you’ll be fine. But if a friend is so drunk that they’ve lost consciousness, are vomiting uncontrollably, or have banged their head, take them to A&E. “There is a small risk of a subdural haematoma [bleeding around the brain] without knowing.”

Diarrhoea only, you’ll most likely be fine within 48 hours. Some stomach bugs can cause blood in your poo, but that’s unusual and you should consult a doctor. Eat bland, dry food and drink flavoured fluids (squash, stock) to replace salts and sugar, not just water. Persistent vomiting is riskier and you shouldn’t eat for 24 hours, stick with the flavoured fluids (little sips but often), but seek medical advice if the vomiting doesn’t settle or you can’t keep any fluids down. Be vigilant with hand hygiene and don’t prepare food for other people until you’re completely better.

On injuries – is it broken? “Seek help if it’s very swollen, or painful to weight-bear, and doesn’t settle with ice compression.”

Animal bites? “Especially if they’re penetrating rather than just a scratch, you should contact a GP promptly as they usually need prophylactic antibiotics.”

If in doubt about what temperature to wash at, most modern washing powders do a good enough job on a cold wash (it’s often a snowflake symbol).

Hang up your towels to dry (spread out flat) after a shower. Then you can use them more than once.

Wash your bedding every two weeks. Realistically, every month is fine, unless you’re entertaining frequently, in which case, every week.

If you leave your washing in the machine too long (say for the entire day), it takes on a weird mouldy smell, and people don’t like that.

Never be the person who thinks someone else in the accommodation is going to do their washing-up. It’s such a dick move.

If you leave a toilet with any visible sign that you’ve been there, someone will be taking a picture of that and putting it in a WhatsApp group that you’re not in.

Whatever you’ve got to put on your wall, you need seven times as many things. Every prison room you’ve seen on TV, that’s what a university room is like.

If you’re going to have plants, water them, otherwise you’ll look like a weirdo.

Does anyone know where you’re going and what time you think you’ll be back? Don’t get too hung up on it, but it’s good if someone has a vague idea.

Nobody knows you well enough to have taken against you. So if everyone’s going to a thing and you’re not sure if you’re invited, just say, “Am I allowed to come to this thing?”

You’re going to meet a lot of people who aren’t like you, haven’t grown up in a nearby street, don’t have the same set of references, don’t have the same associations. Try to accentuate the positives – they haven’t brought their gun with them – and don’t overreact.

Anything with blood goes at the bottom of the fridge (although fridge-sharing between vegetarians and meat-eaters should be negotiated first thing).

Something quick that has protein in it and is not toast. Suggestion: an omelette.

Something that you can make for others that is comforting and nobody can take against or be allergic to. Suggestion: risotto .
Something that you can just pour boiling water over, like a cup of tea, only it’s food. Suggestion: miso soup or soba noodles.

It is actually quite hard to integrate fruit and vegetables into your diet if you’re cooking for yourself but don’t want to spend a lot of time on it. They don’t just magic themselves into food. You should keep a stock of things you can mainline raw while you’re doing something else – carrots, apples, tomatoes, cucumbers.

Everything is edible with the right chilli sauce: harissa, Tabasco, piripiri, sriracha, or for special occasions Hungarian pista or crispy prawn chilli oil. Likewise, pickles: lime pickle, gherkins, jalapeños.
You will probably be about 40 before you can be trusted to spontaneously grate ginger. Pastes in jars or tubes are a cheap alternative: arrive with one garlic and one ginger.
Dr Imogen Bloor, who recently retired as a full-time GP and clinical lead in London, is the source of this expertise.

If you were at home and something happened, you would ask a parent. So call a parent.
Pharmacists can see and treat a whole range of conditions, from hay fever to urinary tract infections. Calling 111 can be helpful, as they can provide advice and signpost you to appropriate services.
Is it freshers’ flu? “As a general principle, if you’ve got mild symptoms and you take paracetamol and fluids and you rest and things seem to improve, that’s a good sign.”

articles.title: US fashion CEO resigns after physically restraining animal rights activists
articles.summary: Steven Kolb of the Council of Fashion Designers of America was filmed during an altercation at New York fashion week The chief executive of the Council of Fashion Designers of America, Steven Kolb, has resigned after he was filmed physically restraining two animal rights activists during an altercation at New York fashion week. “After 20 years leading the CFDA, I have made the difficult decision to step down as CEO and president,” Kolb said in a statement. “I am enormously proud of what we have built together and believe this is the right moment for both me and the organisation to begin a new chapter.” Continue reading...
articles.content:
Steven Kolb of the Council of Fashion Designers of America was filmed during an altercation at New York fashion week

The chief executive of the Council of Fashion Designers of America, Steven Kolb, has resigned after he was filmed physically restraining two animal rights activists during an altercation at New York fashion week .

“After 20 years leading the CFDA, I have made the difficult decision to step down as CEO and president,” Kolb said in a statement. “I am enormously proud of what we have built together and believe this is the right moment for both me and the organisation to begin a new chapter.”

Kolb had been placed on leave on Tuesday pending a review of an incident during a COS show at New York fashion week on Sunday.

In a video , Kolb could be seen trying to restrain two People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta) protesters who attempted to disrupt the show in a demonstration against the use of wool by the H&M group, which owns COS.

Kolb pushed a protester, identified as Mason Melito, and covered his mouth. Kolb also wrestled a second protester to the ground, using his arms and a leg to restrain her and putting his hand over her mouth.

Speaking to the Guardian after the incident, Melito described the situation as scary and said Kolb’s behaviour had been “completely uncalled for”.

The CFDA is a non-profit organisation that supports and promotes US designers and brands. It also organises the official New York fashion week schedule.

A statement issued by the CFDA board, which includes designers such as Ralph Lauren, Thom Browne, Tory Burch and Michael Kors, said: “Steven Kolb has been a dedicated leader and tireless champion of American fashion throughout his more than two decades at the CFDA, including 15 years as CEO.

“We respect Steven’s decision to step down and are grateful for his many years of leadership and service to the CFDA and our industry. He leaves the organisation well positioned, with a clear mission and dedicated team, to carry out the important work ahead as we look to the future of American fashion.”

A Peta USA spokesperson said in a statement: “This unfortunate incident, which has cost Mr Kolb his job, would never have taken place if Daniel Ervér, CEO of H&M, had, as Peta requested so many times, taken action to avoid extreme violence to animals exploited for clothing.

“We will still be meeting with Mr Kolb, and hopefully others in the industry will meet and take meaningful steps to stop this epidemic of cruelty to animals for nothing more than a look.”

Peta staged another protest on Thursday night during London fashion week when three protesters stormed the catwalk during an H&M show. Each one held a sign stating “H&M: Wool is bloody cruel. Drop it.” After stepping down from the catwalk, they were escorted out of the venue by security.

articles.title: China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenario
articles.summary: Silicon Valley China hawks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei among them, fear the country surpassing US’s AI lead as much as superintelligence destroying humanity When reporters asked Donald Trump this week if he supported calls to slow down the development of artificial intelligence out of growing fears for cybersecurity, public safety and the fate of humanity, he said no. His argument: China. “We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to ⁠keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.” Continue reading...
articles.content:
Silicon Valley China hawks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei among them, fear the country surpassing US’s AI lead as much as superintelligence destroying humanity

When reporters asked Donald Trump this week if he supported calls to slow down the development of artificial intelligence out of growing fears for cybersecurity, public safety and the fate of humanity, he said no. His argument: China .

“We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to ⁠keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.”

Trump was echoing a message the AI industry has put out for years. The US is in a heated technological race with China, companies including Anthropic and OpenAI have argued , and any regulation that would cede the contest risks incalculable economic and political harm.

Even as Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, led an industry-wide call this week to “pace the frontier”, he declared that the US could only slow down to the point where China could not catch up.

“If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance,” Amodei warned.

The AI industry’s concerns about China may come with self-serving economic incentives, but they also reflect a strain of hawkish foreign policy toward Beijing that has become entrenched in tech.

In recent years, parts of Silicon Valley have positioned themselves as the vanguard in a new cold war with China, arguing fiercely that the industry’s technological advancements are essential to both US hegemony and the liberal world order. This view has taken hold across tech’s different ideological camps, creating strange bedfellows of AI safety advocates, techno-militarists and neoconservatives, all of them fearful of Beijing.

AI companies have hired former top US government staffers from both the Biden and Trump administrations to shape public strategy and analyze geopolitical risk, setting up in-house policy teams. Influential tech leaders have meanwhile written essays and policy documents calling for efforts to deter and degrade China’s AI capabilities, sometimes advocating for threatening armed conflict if necessary, in an attempt to influence foreign policy.

As public calls for reining in the AI industry intensify and the risks associated with the technology increase, various industry forces are trying to ensure they are the ones with the answer to the question “what about China?”.

Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment for this article.

Few have been more vocal about the threat of Chinese state-controlled artificial intelligence than Amodei. The Anthropic CEO has argued for years that one of the reasons he’s so animated to advance AI is to ensure that the technology falls into the hands of Democratic governments and not oppressive regimes such as China.

Amodei’s position has made him one of Silicon Valley’s most vocal critics of China’s tech industry, separating him from fellow AI leaders such as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman or Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg, who frame the competition more in corporate or economic terms; and people such as Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO, who have encouraged the use of Chinese AI models. Demis Hassabis, the leader of Google Deepmind, has made few public remarks on China in comparison with his peers.

“Sam Altman doesn’t have especially strong views when it comes to China. Anthropic is a totally different story,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution. “Amodei is really, really focused on a particular view of the risk from AI and what he frames as basically a struggle between a world dominated by authoritarian AI versus democratic AI”.

Amodei’s argument, which he has laid out over a series of essays, is that China acquiring superpowered AI is one of the most severe threats posed by the technology. He believes humanity is approaching the creation of an ultra-advanced AI, and that such a tool would give an authoritarian state the ability to create a “swarm of millions or billions of fully automated armed drones” that would be “capable of both defeating any military in the world and suppressing dissent within a country by following around every citizen”.

“There are a number of possible arguments against the severity of these threats, and I wish I believed them, because AI-enabled authoritarianism terrifies me,” Amodei wrote in January in an essay called The Adolescence of Technology.

Amodei has long asserted that in order to stop China’s advancement, the US and its allies should take aggressive action to limit Chinese AI companies’ growth – most notably blocking the sale of advanced semiconductor chips and manufacturing equipment necessary for improving AI. (Huang of Nvidia has bristled at this position, calling export controls a failure and urging Trump to ease restrictions.)

But Amodei’s position was perhaps most on display last weekend, in his response to warnings from a young Anthropic researcher who resigned, predicting human extinction by the end of the decade at the digital hands of AI. The apocalyptic string of tweets by Jacob Coxon did not mention China. But the specter across the Pacific looms so large in the Anthropic CEO’s mind that, when outlining how to prevent human extinction, beating Beijing was paramount.

Amodei has built a team that shares his views. He for example hired Tarun Chhabra, former Biden-era national security council staffer, as Anthropic’s head of national security policy. Chhabra has campaigned against the sale of chips to China and has called for a full-scale government effort to curb the Chinese Communist party’s AI advancements.

“The CCP does not seek complementarity or coexistence or comparative advantage with the United States or our allies. Instead, the CCP seeks run-the-table dominance and control of the most critical technologies and supply chains,” Chhabra told a Senate hearing last year, adding that he believed the Biden administration did not take decisive or rapid enough action to maintain the US lead against China.

Amodei’s concern over export controls has also placed him in the company of other influential China hawks. He wrote an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal last year with Matt Pottinger, the architect of Trump’s first-term China policy, urging the administration to clamp down on chip exports. Pottinger, a visiting fellow at the conservative Hoover Institution and author of a book on how to defend Taiwan against a Chinese attack, argued in 2024 that the US and China were in the “foothills of a great-power hot war”.

Anthropic and Amodei’s stance on China puts the company in strange tension with its own domestic policy. The company has spent millions lobbying for increased government oversight and safety measures. At the same time as Anthropic advocates for more safeguards, it has made clear that it will aggressively oppose any policy it perceives as giving China the chance to overtake the US.

“There’s something that’s really important that everyone hears from Anthropic,” Sarah Heck, the company’s head of public policy, said at a Politico event on Wednesday. “The United States needs to stay in the lead on AI and you cannot do safety from second place.”

Understanding the beliefs of AI companies and CEOs such as Amodei is particularly important, experts say, because the Trump administration’s laissez faire policy towards the AI industry has meant that private companies are the primary actors in shaping public policy.

“It would be akin to having the entire pharmaceutical industry be just completely unregulated,” Chan said. “It’s kind of amazing and ultimately boils down to one thing, which is Trump has been very reluctant to want to regulate because he doesn’t want to slow down the AI boom and the effect that it’s having on the economy.”

Anthropic is not the only company to hire and align with former top policy staffers, with OpenAI hiring the author of Trump’s AI action plan Dean Ball as “head of strategic futures” earlier this year. While Ball has criticized Amodei’s framing of the competition with China,, he has expressed a similar pessimism on US-China cooperation.

“There was a time when it was possible to believe we could each pursue our strengths, enrich our respective economies, and grow together. Alas, such harmony now appears impossible,” Ball wrote of China last year. “We are locked into a structural conflict.”

Although Amodei is the AI industry’s most prominent voice on China, fears of Beijing gaining advanced AI capabilities and using them for global domination run through Silicon Valley.

Several of the tech figures focused on China have connections, like Amodei himself, to the effective altruism movement – a quasi-utilitarian idea that society should focus on projects that maximize the good and reduce the most harm for humanity. The movement tends to overlap with AI safety advocates who worry about the longterm, existential risks of the technology.

Leopold Aschenbrenner, a 25-year-old former OpenAI researcher, founder of an influential AI hedge fund, and husband to Amodei’s chief of staff, called for a government-led effort to reach super-intelligent AI before China in a 165-page paper.

“Super-intelligence will give a decisive economic and military advantage. China isn’t at all out of the game yet. In the race to AGI, the free world’s very survival will be at stake,” Aschenbrenner wrote in 2024.

The position of Aschenbrenner, who made headlines earlier this year when his hedge fund lost $35bn in less than a month, was echoed in Washington. When the typically hawkish US-China cconomic and security review commission issued its annual report to Congress a few months after Aschenbrenner’s manifesto, the congressional advisory committee’s number one suggestion was to “establish and fund a Manhattan Project-like program dedicated to racing to and acquiring an Artificial General Intelligence”.

Grand strategy proposals from the AI industry on China are not solely contained within the effective altruist movement. In 2025, Google co-founder Eric Schmidt, Alexander Wang, Scale AI founder (now head of AI at Meta), and Dan Hendrycks, Center for AI Safety director, wrote a wide-ranging strategic deterrence doctrine called Mutual Assured AI Malfunction (Maim). Their paper applies the cold war framework of Mutually Assured Destruction (Mad) with nuclear weapons and applies it to AI, proposing that the US and China could achieve geopolitical stability through threatening espionage, cyberattacks and potential military strikes against each other if either state pursues a monopoly on AI.

“A nation with sole possession of super-intelligence might be as overwhelming as the Conquistadors were to the Aztecs,” the paper warns.

Some leading AI thinkers have argued for extreme measures to deal with AI advancement from nations such as China. Eliezer Yudkowsky, one of the earliest and loudest voices of the AI safety movement, has argued that the US should be willing to carry out airstrikes against foreign data centers and risk nuclear war in order to make rival states comply with a global AI moratorium.

“Make it explicit in international diplomacy that preventing AI extinction scenarios is considered a priority above preventing a full nuclear exchange, and that allied nuclear countries are willing to run some risk of nuclear exchange if that’s what it takes to reduce the risk of large AI training runs,” Yudkowsky wrote in a 2023 Time Magazine essay .

Yudkowsky founded the Machine Research Intelligence Institute, which has received more than $10m in funding over the past decade from Open Philanthropy, a non-profit associated with the effective altruism movement. Open Philanthropy’s cofounder and former CEO Holden Karnovsky is married to Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei.

Other China hawks in the tech and AI industry tend to have ties to the military industrial complex and an economic incentive in the competition, such as Anduril founder Palmer Luckey and Palantir CEO Alex Karp. Luckey has claimed that his defense tech firm has an internal policy that any of its projects need to be built with the assumption China will launch hostilities against Taiwan in 2027.

Karp has meanwhile framed the AI competition with China as a fight for geopolitical supremacy and suggested Americans should accept tradeoffs to their civil liberties to win.

“We are going to be the dominant player or China is going to be the dominant player. And there will be very different rules depending on who wins,” Karp told Axios last year. “When people are worried about surveillance, of course there are huge dangers there, but it’s like, you will have far fewer rights if America is not in the lead.”

While Amodei and other US AI leaders frame competition with China as a race to reach a super-powerful artificial intelligence first and worry about AI breaking free of human control, experts say that most Chinese firms and their government don’t view the technology the same way. Instead, loss of control debates are relatively new in China, and the government’s primary concern is how AI could lead to domestic social unrest.

As China and the US are set to hold talks this month on AI cooperation, experts say Beijing is primarily approaching the talks from a place of distrust that the negotiations are merely a way to suppress its growth under the guise of safety. Amodei’s essay has fueled that concern.

“They’re very much paying attention to Amodei’s essay and they’re also conflating his essay with potential US approach in the upcoming AI safety talks,” said Kenton Thibaut, senior resident China fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Digital Forensic Research Lab. Trump is set to meet with Xi Jinping in less than a week in Washington, with AI high on the agenda.

China’s state-backed media properties have aggressively criticized Amodei, accusing him of running a “cold war playbook” against China through his support for an AI slowdown. Experts say Anthropic’s dual calls for both strict export controls on China and safety agreements have also had the effect of combining the discourse around two arguably separate subjects: AI safety and economic competition around AI.

“Anthropic has played quite a strong role here in linking those issues together in a way that they maybe didn’t need to be linked,” Brookings’ Chan said. “To put it really bluntly, it made it much harder to get the Chinese to want to talk about these things and not see it purely as a veiled way to slow them down.”

While the Trump administration negotiates with China, the growing domestic backlash to the AI industry in the US may force lawmakers to take action regardless of how it affects global power dynamics. Nationwide opposition to datacenters and recent cybersecurity incidents such as OpenAI’s models hacking into outside organizations have become midterm election topics, adding incentive for lawmakers to to address the immediate harms related to AI.

“You can go ahead and wield the China arms race argument, but at some point this industry will also have to deal with the consequences of fueling a race to the bottom,” said Amba Kak, co-executive director at the AI Now Institute and former senior adviser on AI for the Federal Trade Commission.

Although experts and diplomats have expressed little hope that upcoming US-China talks will lead to major agreements, it is also possible that the increasingly real risks of AI being used for autonomous weapons, cyberattacks and other destabilizing technologies may force countries to shift the AI race’s course even if they don’t stop building it.

“We don’t win if we develop the killer robots first. Nobody wants killer robots,” Thibaut said. “There should be powerful incentives on both sides to stop this.”

When reporters asked Donald Trump this week if he supported calls to slow down the development of artificial intelligence out of growing fears for cybersecurity, public safety and the fate of humanity, he said no. His argument: China .
“We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to ⁠keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.”

Trump was echoing a message the AI industry has put out for years. The US is in a heated technological race with China, companies including Anthropic and OpenAI have argued , and any regulation that would cede the contest risks incalculable economic and political harm.
Even as Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, led an industry-wide call this week to “pace the frontier”, he declared that the US could only slow down to the point where China could not catch up.

“If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance,” Amodei warned.
The AI industry’s concerns about China may come with self-serving economic incentives, but they also reflect a strain of hawkish foreign policy toward Beijing that has become entrenched in tech.

In recent years, parts of Silicon Valley have positioned themselves as the vanguard in a new cold war with China, arguing fiercely that the industry’s technological advancements are essential to both US hegemony and the liberal world order. This view has taken hold across tech’s different ideological camps, creating strange bedfellows of AI safety advocates, techno-militarists and neoconservatives, all of them fearful of Beijing.

AI companies have hired former top US government staffers from both the Biden and Trump administrations to shape public strategy and analyze geopolitical risk, setting up in-house policy teams. Influential tech leaders have meanwhile written essays and policy documents calling for efforts to deter and degrade China’s AI capabilities, sometimes advocating for threatening armed conflict if necessary, in an attempt to influence foreign policy.

As public calls for reining in the AI industry intensify and the risks associated with the technology increase, various industry forces are trying to ensure they are the ones with the answer to the question “what about China?”.
Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment for this article.

Few have been more vocal about the threat of Chinese state-controlled artificial intelligence than Amodei. The Anthropic CEO has argued for years that one of the reasons he’s so animated to advance AI is to ensure that the technology falls into the hands of Democratic governments and not oppressive regimes such as China.

Amodei’s position has made him one of Silicon Valley’s most vocal critics of China’s tech industry, separating him from fellow AI leaders such as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman or Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg, who frame the competition more in corporate or economic terms; and people such as Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO, who have encouraged the use of Chinese AI models. Demis Hassabis, the leader of Google Deepmind, has made few public remarks on China in comparison with his peers.

The company has spent millions lobbying for increased government oversight and safety measures. At the same time as Anthropic advocates for more safeguards, it has made clear that it will aggressively oppose any policy it perceives as giving China the chance to overtake the US.

“There’s something that’s really important that everyone hears from Anthropic,” Sarah Heck, the company’s head of public policy, said at a Politico event on Wednesday. “The United States needs to stay in the lead on AI and you cannot do safety from second place.”

Understanding the beliefs of AI companies and CEOs such as Amodei is particularly important, experts say, because the Trump administration’s laissez faire policy towards the AI industry has meant that private companies are the primary actors in shaping public policy.

“It would be akin to having the entire pharmaceutical industry be just completely unregulated,” Chan said. “It’s kind of amazing and ultimately boils down to one thing, which is Trump has been very reluctant to want to regulate because he doesn’t want to slow down the AI boom and the effect that it’s having on the economy.”

Anthropic is not the only company to hire and align with former top policy staffers, with OpenAI hiring the author of Trump’s AI action plan Dean Ball as “head of strategic futures” earlier this year. articles.title: Alex de Minaur roars back to life as Australia and Poland share spoils in Davis Cup
articles.summary: World No 9 beats Maks Kasnikowski 6-3, 6-0 in World Group I tie James Duckworth loses to Kamil Majchrzak 2-6, 6-3, 6-3 in Brisbane Alex de Minaur has taken his frustrations out in a Davis Cup thumping to put Australia up 1-0 in their must-win Brisbane tie against Poland, before Kamil Majchrzak edged James Duckworth in a tense two-hour affair. The world No 9, keen to rediscover his mojo after a disappointing second-round US Open loss , lit up Pat Rafter Arena on Saturday afternoon with a dominant 6-3 6-0 defeat of world No 231 Maks Kasnikowski. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Alex de Minaur has taken his frustrations out in a Davis Cup thumping to put Australia up 1-0 in their must-win Brisbane tie against Poland, before Kamil Majchrzak edged James Duckworth in a tense two-hour affair.

The world No 9, keen to rediscover his mojo after a disappointing second-round US Open loss , lit up Pat Rafter Arena on Saturday afternoon with a dominant 6-3 6-0 defeat of world No 231 Maks Kasnikowski.

But the tie is all square after Brisbane home town hero Duckworth was defeated by Majchrzak 2-6, 6-3, 6-3 in the second singles match, before Sunday’s doubles and reverse singles.

The first singles match lasted 56 minutes and de Minaur lost just six points in the second set as the Australian No 1 found range on his serve, angles from the baseline and got to the net to finish points with authority.

De Minaur roared after breaking for the first time in the fourth game and then, after a tight call went against him with his tail up at 4-1, steadied with back-to-back aces.

Kasnikowski saved two set points on serve and forced de Minaur to serve out the first set, which he did with ease before breaking instantly to set the tone for a one-sided second set.

“That’s what these ties are all about; get fired up, get the crowd involved and there’s no better feeling,” de Minaur said of his theatrics.

“We play outside of Australia for 10 months a year … so being here, in front of a packed crowd, great atmosphere it’s one I’ve missed.

“The serve felt great … I had some nice words to it and it’s coming out to play.”

Kasnikowski admits he was blown away in his first meeting with a member of the world’s top 10.

“It was a unique experience. A really, really tough challenge and happy I put up a little bit of a fight in the first set,” he said.

“In the second, Alex increased the level a lot and it was too much for me today.

The hosts looked set to surge ahead 2-0 when Duckworth peeled off five straight games to take the first set and then break early in the third.

But Majchrzak broke straight back, then saved two more break points at 3-3, before a string of unforced errors cost Duckworth in his next service game.

Sunday’s doubles will be pivotal before de Minaur and Majchrzak meet, just months after the Polish talent beat the Australian in a tight, three-set final in ‘s-Hertogenbosch.

If the tie is split 2-2, Duckworth and Kasnikowski are slated to play the decisive fifth rubber, with the winners progressing to next year’s qualifying round and the losers eliminated altogether from the 2027 Cup race that culminates in Italy next November.

Australia were upset in Ecuador earlier this year and must win this clash to progress to next year’s qualifying round, where they can then book a place in the eight-team finals in Italy in November.
